reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: A mass of non-functioning lung tissue that lacks a normal connection to the tracheobronchial tree and derives its blood supply from an anomalous systemic artery
The defining feature is a systemic feeding vessel, typically arising from the descending thoracic or upper abdominal aorta

Intralobar sequestration lies within the visceral pleura of a normal lobe and drains to pulmonary veins, whereas extralobar sequestration has its own pleural covering and usually systemic venous drainage
Often identified antenatally as a solid, well-defined echogenic lung lesion, frequently in the left lower zone
Extralobar lesions are more often found in neonates and may be associated with other anomalies such as diaphragmatic hernia
Intralobar lesions more commonly present later with recurrent infection in the same region of lung
Definitive imaging demonstrates the systemic feeding artery, and symptomatic or persistent lesions are treated by resection with careful control of the aberrant vessel
reference.pathophysiology: Bronchopulmonary sequestration is thought to arise from an accessory lung bud that develops caudal to the normal lung, migrating with the developing foregut and retaining a primitive systemic arterial supply from the aorta rather than acquiring a normal pulmonary connection. The sequestered tissue therefore does not participate in gas exchange and lacks normal bronchial communication. In extralobar sequestration the accessory tissue has its own pleural investment and systemic venous drainage, while in intralobar sequestration the abnormal tissue is incorporated within a normal lobe and tends to drain via pulmonary veins. Absent normal airway clearance predisposes intralobar lesions to recurrent infection, and hybrid lesions sharing features with congenital pulmonary airway malformation are recognised.
additionalDifferentials: Neuroblastoma or other posterior mediastinal mass
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal ultrasound identifying an echogenic lung mass, with Doppler seeking a systemic feeding vessel
Fetal MRI for lesion characterisation when needed
Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest to define the aberrant artery and venous drainage
Chest radiograph, recognising it may be subtle or show a persistent basal opacity
MRI or CT to distinguish it from other posterior thoracic masses
Histology of the resected specimen for confirmation and to identify hybrid features
redFlags: Recurrent or severe infection within the sequestered segment
High-output cardiac failure from a large systemic arteriovenous shunt
Fetal hydrops from a large lesion or associated effusion
Neonatal respiratory distress from mass effect
Haemorrhage risk from an unrecognised large systemic feeding artery at surgery
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally excellent after complete resection, which is curative and prevents recurrent infection and shunt-related complications. Large fetal lesions causing hydrops carry a poorer outlook, and outcome may be influenced by coexisting anomalies, particularly with extralobar disease.
pitfalls: Failing to identify and securely control the anomalous systemic artery, risking major haemorrhage
Misclassifying the lesion as ordinary recurrent pneumonia and delaying definitive imaging
Overlooking associated anomalies such as diaphragmatic hernia with extralobar lesions
Confusing it with congenital pulmonary airway malformation without seeking the systemic vessel
Assuming a normal chest radiograph excludes a sequestration seen antenatally
management: Offer definitive surgical resection with careful ligation of the anomalous systemic feeding artery, which is curative and prevents recurrent infection and shunt complications
Define the aberrant arterial supply and venous drainage preoperatively with CT angiography to plan safe surgery
Treat any superimposed infection with antibiotics before elective resection
Monitor antenatally, offering foetal intervention such as a thoracoamniotic shunt for large lesions causing hydrops
Assess for associated congenital anomalies, particularly diaphragmatic hernia in extralobar lesions
Refer to paediatric surgery and manage within a multidisciplinary team
